title: Occasion, date and addressee
short: A verse letter of late 1714 to Teresa Blount, sent back to the country after the coronation of George I on 20 October 1714.
body: George I was crowned at Westminster on 20 October 1714, and the festivities brought the Catholic gentry, briefly, into London society. Teresa Blount (1688-1759) and her sister Martha, Pope's close friends from Mapledurham near Reading, had to return to the country afterwards. The poem was first printed in Pope's Works of 1717 as 'To the same, on her leaving the Town after the Coronation', following the epistle that accompanied a gift of Voiture's works; 'the same' is Miss Blount. The addressee is generally identified as Teresa, since 'Zephalinda' was her coterie name, and the archive's title names her; her sister Martha is the likelier 'Parthenia' of l. 46. The poem's teasing affection has been read in the light of Pope's shifting feelings for both sisters.

title: Mock-epic simile
short: The opening 'As ... Thus' construction borrows the shape of the epic simile for a fashionable young woman's departure from town.
body: Homer and Virgil introduce a comparison with 'as when' and close it with 'so' or 'thus'. Pope uses the same frame on a tiny scale: a girl dragged from a flirtation by her mother is the vehicle, and Zephalinda's departure is the tenor. The comedy lies in the disproportion, a technique Pope was perfecting at the same time in The Rape of the Lock (1714). 'The world' here means fashionable society, the beau monde, as opposed to the country. Note too that the simile is itself a small story with a kiss 'before she parts for ever', so that the exaggerated pathos of 'for ever' is gently mocked.

title: a melting eye
short: A languishing, amorous glance; the girl is just learning the arts of the coquette.
body: 'Melting' in the sense 'tender, languishing, softened by love' was a standard term of amatory verse and drama in Pope's day, and to 'roll' the eyes was the conventional stage gesture of a woman in love. The phrase is therefore slightly ironic: the girl has learned the outward signs of feeling as a social skill, just as she is learning to 'hear a spark' without noticing the risk. Pope's Eloisa to Abelard (1717) uses the same vocabulary seriously; here it belongs to the light satire of manners.

title: spark
short: A spark is a showy young man about town, a beau or gallant; 'hear' implies listening to his compliments.
body: The OED records 'spark' in the sense of an elegant or foppish young man, often a lover, from the late sixteenth century; it was common in Restoration comedy. To 'hear a spark' is to listen to his addresses, and 'yet think no danger nigh' points to the mother's reason for removing her daughter to 'wholesome country air'. The moral language (danger, wholesome) is put in the mother's mouth and teased; the poem's sympathy lies with the girl's regret.

title: Zephalinda
short: Teresa Blount's romance name in the sisters' circle, used in 1713 in the circle of James Moore Smythe.
body: Coterie names drawn from French heroic romance were fashionable among young women and their admirers. In 1713 the sisters corresponded with James Moore Smythe, author of the comedy The Rival Modes, in which he figures as 'Alexis', Teresa as 'Zephalinda' and Martha as 'Parthenissa'. Pope adopts the name to give the epistle the air of a romance heroine's lament while using an in-joke the addressee would recognise. The romance name also fits the poem's theme: the lady's imagination keeps turning her country life into a scene from fiction.

title: Antithesis and the couplet
short: The balanced line sets 'staid' against 'went': she envies no one their pleasure, she only regrets her own loss of it.
body: 'Staid' is the usual eighteenth-century spelling of 'stayed'. The couplet is a model of the Augustan heroic couplet, closed and pointed, with the antithesis divided at the caesura. Its wit is a kind act of defence: Zephalinda is cleared of envy, but in a way that confesses how much she wanted to remain. The phrase 'she went' is then picked up as an anaphora in the next paragraph ('She went to ... She went from'), turning the regret into a comic itinerary of rural boredom.

title: plain-work; purling brooks
short: Plain-work is ordinary sewing as opposed to fancy embroidery; 'purling brooks' is a stock phrase of pastoral verse.
body: The OED defines 'plain work' as plain needlework, the hemming and seaming of household linen, as distinct from decorative work. Pairing it with 'purling brooks' (murmuring streams) yokes domestic drudgery with the pastoral clichés of country poetry, and the line ends with 'croaking rooks', the noisy birds of rookeries near old country houses. Pope himself mocked 'purling streams' as a cliché of bad pastoral; here the phrase measures the gap between the poetic idea of the country and its reality for a young woman.

title: Pleasures of the town
short: A list of the London season's diversions: Italian opera, the fashionable promenade in the parks, evening assemblies and the theatre.
body: Italian opera had become a craze in London from about 1705, and Handel's Rinaldo (1711) sealed its fashion. The 'park' is Hyde Park or St James's Park, where the fashionable walked and drove; an 'assembly' was an evening gathering of polite company for cards, conversation and dancing. The line moves in four quick beats, and the next line answers with the country day: 'morning-walks, and prayers three hours a-day', the long devotions of a pious Catholic household. The two lists set London's evening pleasures against rural morning duties.

title: bohea
short: A black China tea, named from the Wuyi (Bu-i) hills in Fujian; pronounced to rhyme with 'tea'.
body: The OED records 'bohea' from the early eighteenth century as the name of a black tea from the Wuyi hills of Fujian province, at first a fine grade and later a cheap one. Tea was still a luxury in 1714 and associated with women's sociability; to drink it alone, as here, empties it of its social purpose. The couplet's rhyme 'bohea / tea' follows the period pronunciation, in which 'tea' was often sounded 'tay', as in The Rape of the Lock's rhyme of 'tea' with 'obey'.

title: Solitary tea and cold coffee
short: Small actions of boredom: absent-mindedly spilling her tea, stirring cold coffee, counting the hours.
body: The comedy of these lines is bathos: 'To muse' is a dignified, poetic activity, and it is followed at once by the clumsiness of spilling the tea. Coffee left to go cold and a spoon used only to 'trifle' show time that has nothing to fill it, and the next line's 'Count the slow clock' makes the theme explicit. The detail of dining 'exact at noon' marks the country timetable, earlier and more regular than the fashionable London hour for dinner, which was moving later in the afternoon in this period. Pope's eye for domestic minutiae anticipates the novel of manners.

title: pictures in the fire
short: Seeing shapes in the glowing coals, a pastime of idle evenings; it prepares for the lady's day-dream of coronations later.
body: Looking for faces and scenes in the fire was a proverbial idle amusement. It is a small instance of fancy, and it looks forward to the third paragraph, where Zephalinda dreams of the coronation in 'imaginary sights'. 'Hum half a tune' and 'tell stories to the 'squire' complete the picture of a mind half-occupied; the poem ends with the poet himself humming a tune, so the motif returns in the last line.

title: starve
short: To 'starve' could mean to suffer from cold as well as hunger; the unheated garret makes both senses apt.
body: The OED records the older sense of 'starve', to die or suffer from cold, which survived in dialect long after the hunger sense dominated. A 'godly garret' is a cold attic bedroom given a mock-pious epithet, and bedtime 'after seven' is absurdly early by town standards. The couplet closes the paragraph with a comic aphorism ('for that's the way to heaven') that glances at the Blounts' devout Catholic household without real hostility; Pope, himself a Catholic, is mocking rural austerity rather than religion.

title: The country squire
short: A comic portrait of the rough rural suitor, the stock booby squire of comedy, whom she 'racks' (torments) with her coquetry.
body: The apostrophe in 'squire marks it as an abbreviation of 'esquire'. The country squire, hard-drinking, hunting and boorish, was a stock figure in Restoration and early eighteenth-century comedy and in periodical essays such as the Spectator's portrait of Sir Roger de Coverley (a gentler version). 'Rack' means to torture, as on the rack, and is the language of romance: the lady's only power in the country is to torment her clumsy admirer. The portrait is built of telling details: he courts with dead game, nods and knee-pressing under the table.

anchor: whose treat, a toast in sack
title: whist; a toast in sack
short: Whist was then a homely card game; 'sack' a Spanish or Canary white wine, and a toast here possibly literal toasted bread dipped in it.
body: In 1714 whist was considered an unfashionable game of country houses and servants' halls; it became fashionable later in the century. 'Sack' was the general name for dry white wines imported from Spain and the Canaries, Falstaff's drink. A 'toast in sack' may be the drinking of her health, or a piece of toast soaked in wine, a common old-fashioned dish; editors note both possibilities, and either way the 'treat' is unrefined. The comic point is that the squire's pleasures are as old-fashioned as the country halls in l. 12.

title: smacking buss; No words!
short: A buss is a loud, hearty kiss; 'No words!' means 'Say nothing about it', a conspirator's whisper.
body: The OED records 'buss' as a rough or playful kiss, a low word by Pope's time; 'smacking' adds the sound. 'No words!' is a colloquial injunction to secrecy. The country lover's kiss answers the 'one kiss' of the opening simile (l. 6), but crude where the other was sentimental. The squire 'visits with a gun' and brings 'birds' (game he has shot) as love-tokens, the sporting gentleman's courtship.

title: Anticlimax
short: The paragraph ends on bathos: the squire loves her best of all things, except his horse.
body: The dash before the last two words sets up the anticlimax, a favourite device of Pope's satire (compare the 'Puffs, Powders, Patches, Bibles, Billet-doux' of The Rape of the Lock). The pointed final line sums up the rural suitor's priorities and the fate of a woman of wit in the country. Readers have noted that the joke is affectionate rather than cruel, and that it gives Zephalinda the power to mock her suitor that she lacks in the life she has been sent back to.

title: The day-dream of coronations
short: Alone in the evening she dreams of the coronation splendours; a flick of her fan ends the vision.
body: This paragraph is a miniature of the 'vision' passages of romance and of Pope's own Rape of the Lock. 'Triumphs' are pageants or processions, and 'garter'd knights' are Knights of the Garter in their insignia, who walked in the coronation procession. 'Coronets' are the small crowns worn by peers at a coronation. The vision rises 'on every green', so the country is briefly transformed into court, and then 'all the vision flies'. The close, 'lone woods, or empty walls', is gently mock-tragic, the forsaken romance heroine in her solitude.

title: flirt
short: A flirt is a sudden jerk or flick, here of the fan; the modern sense of amorous trifling was also current, and is in play.
body: The OED gives 'flirt' first as a sudden jerk or quick movement, and records 'a flirt of a fan' among its uses; the fan was a woman's instrument of social expression. The verb 'to flirt' in the sense of trifling amorously was also coming into use, and Pope enjoys the ambiguity: the gesture that dispels the vision is itself the coquette's gesture. In the Spectator no. 102 (1711) Addison satirised an 'academy' for the 'exercise of the fan', including the 'flutter' of the fan, a good gloss on the cultural meaning of the gesture.

title: The poet's turn
short: Pope now describes himself, the lady's 'slave' in the language of gallantry, day-dreaming of her in the London streets.
body: The last paragraph answers the 'As ... Thus' of the opening with a second 'So when': the poet is in town and dreaming of the country lady, as she is in the country dreaming of the town. 'Slave' is the conventional servant of the lover in courtly and romance convention. The parenthesis 'Not plagued with headaches, or the want of rhyme' is self-mockery: Pope suffered from chronic headaches, and the 'want of rhyme' is the poet's occupational complaint. 'Abstracted from the crew' means withdrawn in thought from the crowd.

title: Parthenia
short: Probably Martha Blount, Teresa's younger sister, whose coterie name was 'Parthenissa'; the name implies maidenly modesty.
body: The name derives from Greek parthenos, 'maiden'. In the 1713 names of the Moore Smythe circle Martha was 'Parthenissa', and editors commonly take 'Parthenia' as Martha, so that the poet's day-dream includes both sisters. The 'blush' fits the name's suggestion of modesty. Since Martha was to become Pope's lifelong companion, biographers have found the line suggestive, though in 1714 it is still part of a playful compliment to both women; Rumbold and Mack discuss the shifting relations of Pope with the two sisters.

title: Gay
short: John Gay (1685-1732), poet and Pope's close friend, whose friendly interruption breaks the day-dream.
body: Gay, the future author of The Beggar's Opera (1728), was a fellow member with Pope of the Scriblerus Club, formed in 1714. His poem Trivia, or the Art of Walking the Streets of London (1716) is a mock-georgic of the city's streets, and the line's crowd of 'Streets, chairs, and coxcombs' is just the world of that poem. The tap on the shoulder works like the lady's flirt of the fan: a small physical gesture dispels the vision and returns the dreamer to where he is.

title: chairs; coxcombs
short: Chairs are sedan chairs, carried through London's streets by two chairmen; coxcombs are fops.
body: The sedan chair, a covered seat on poles carried by two men, was the usual way for the well-to-do to move through crowded London streets in the early eighteenth century. 'Coxcomb' (from the jester's cap shaped like a cock's comb) had come to mean a conceited, showy fool, a fop. The line is the urban counterpart of the rural list in l. 12 ('Old-fashion'd halls, dull aunts, and croaking rooks'), each of three items: the town is no more satisfying to the poet than the country is to the lady.

title: The symmetrical close
short: The poet, vexed to be in town, hums a tune and looks sour just as she does in the country; their discontents mirror each other.
body: The final couplet closes the poem's design. Zephalinda in the country longs for town; the poet in town longs for the country because she is there. 'Hum a tune' recalls l. 20, and the present tense 'as you do now' imagines her reading the poem with exactly that expression. The joke turns the satire back on its author, so that the poem's mockery of the lady becomes a shared joke about the restlessness of desire. Critics have admired the poem as one of Pope's most graceful light pieces, combining the satire of manners with intimacy.
